g.text: Event time vs processing time — skew, watermarks, and what completeness costs
max skew 230s (id 7) · watermark lag 60s · waiting 60s drops 1 of 9
HOW LATE EACH EVENT WAS, IN SECONDS
Eight of the nine arrive within 50s. One — id 7 — takes 230s.
Skew is not a constant you can look up. It is a long tail, and the tail is where correctness lives.
Step 1/4 — skew, measured: processing time minus event time
Skew is the single measured quantity this chapter rests on. Note its SHAPE: a cluster of small values and one outlier 5× larger. Any system that
picks a waiting time from the typical case is correct for eight events in nine and silently wrong about the ninth.
Event time vs processing time — skew, watermarks, and what completeness costs
max skew 230s (id 7) · watermark lag 60s · waiting 60s drops 1 of 9
THE WATERMARK AFTER EACH EVENT — max event time seen, minus LAG = 60s
row 1 = the arriving event, in processing order · row 2 = its event time · row 3 = the watermark after it
A watermark is one claim: "no event with an event time earlier than this will arrive." Here it is computed as the highest event time seen so far,
By the time id 7 arrives the watermark stands at 12:03:20, which already claims 12:00:50 is settled. The claim is false. Nothing detected that.
Step 2/4 — the watermark is a GUESS about skew
The watermark never stalls and never apologises — it is arithmetic on the events that did arrive, so it cannot know about one that has not. The
60s lag is a human guess at the skew tail, and id 7's 230s is 4x it. A heuristic watermark being wrong is its normal mode, not a failure.
Event time vs processing time — skew, watermarks, and what completeness costs
max skew 230s (id 7) · watermark lag 60s · waiting 60s drops 1 of 9
two budgets, and what each one buys
Completeness is bought with latency, at a fixed exchange rate: 170s of extra delay on EVERY answer to stop losing 1 event in 9.
Nobody can tell you that is worth it. That is the point — it is a product decision wearing an engineering costume.
Step 3/4 — what completeness costs: wait longer, or drop events
Both rows are correct systems. The first is fast and loses 1 of 9 events; the second is complete and makes every answer 170s later — 680s across
the 4 windows. And the second budget was only knowable AFTER seeing id 7, so in a live system you are choosing it blind.
Event time vs processing time — skew, watermarks, and what completeness costs
max skew 230s (id 7) · watermark lag 60s · waiting 60s drops 1 of 9
the question decides the clock; the clock is never a default
EVENT time — it is a fact about users
"what is our ingest rate right now?"
PROCESSING time — it is a fact about us
"was this user's session longer than 2 min?"
EVENT time — the user's clock, not ours
BOTH — the gap between them IS the lag
Processing time is not the lazy choice — it is the right answer to questions about the SYSTEM.
It is the wrong answer to questions about the WORLD, and those are most of the questions anyone asks.
Step 4/4 — so each clock is correct for a different question
The useful habit is to read the question for whose clock it mentions. "How many clicks happened at 12:00" names the users' clock, so the answer is
12. "How many did we receive in that minute" names ours, so the answer is 8. Both are right; only one of them is what a dashboard labelled "clicks
